extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (esp. Locke / early modern empiricism)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter explaining Locke's account of the origins and nature of the ideas of space, extension, duration, succession, and measures of time. It discusses how we form these ideas by sensation and reflection and what counts as a good measure of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension not identical to body
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension being inseparable from Body, proves it not the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the idea of extension is inseparably joined to many sensible qualities (sight and touch), that constant association does not establish extension as the whole essence of body. One who equates body with extension mistakes frequent co-occurrence for identity; other qualities (tastes, smells, pains) show that bodies can be conceived without extension being their essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of space distinct from solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: We have as clear an idea of space distinct from solidity, as of solidity distinct from motion, or motion from space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Space (considered as extension between coherent parts, as length/breadth/thickness, or as distance between bodies) is a uniform simple idea taken from sensory experience and reflection, and can be conceived either filled with solidity or as void. The text insists on the conceptual distinctness even if existence relations obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration (time) arises from reflection on the train of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of succession and of duration is obtained by reflecting on the train of ideas that appear one after another in our minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that by observing the successive appearance of ideas while awake we form the notion of succession; the distance between two such appearances is duration. This account is supported by examples like sleep (where no perceived succession yields no perception of elapsed duration) and dreaming (where succession and time can be perceived).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of duration depends on continuous succession of ideas while awake
rubrics_metrics.description: When the succession of ideas ceases (e.g., deep sleep), perception of duration ceases; the mind uses the train of ideas as a measure of elapsed time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples: a sleeping person loses perception of elapsed time (an hour or a day seems lost); intensely fixated attention can make time seem shorter because fewer ideas are noticed in succession; dreams can supply a sense of duration during sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession (time) is not derived from motion but from ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of succession is derived from the train of ideas, not directly from motion; motion only gives a sense of succession insofar as it produces successive ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a becalmed ship may be moving but produce no sense of motion unless changes produce successive ideas; conversely, a train of internal ideas suffices to produce the notion of succession even without sensed motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very slow and very swift motions can be unperceived
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions that are either too slow (not supplying a continual train of distinguishable ideas) or too swift (so fast they do not produce distinct successive ideas) are not perceived as motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: clock hands or sundial shadows (very slow) seem at rest though they move; very swift events (a cannon-ball) produce no perceived succession in pain or sound though succession objectively occurred. Such unperceived parts of duration are called an instant (one idea's time).

rubrics_metrics.name: The train of ideas is the measure/standard of other successions
rubrics_metrics.description: The regular succession of ideas in a waking person acts as the measure and standard by which other successions (motions, sounds, pains) are judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an external succession is faster than our ideas, multiple events occupy one idea's duration; if slower, gaps occur and the succession is lost to perception. Locke suggests there are bounds to the quickness and slowness of our ideas' succession, which determine perceptibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good measure of time must divide duration into equal periods
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure time usefully, a measure must divide duration into apparently equal portions; only regularly repeated periods serve well as measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike spatial measures that are static, temporal measures require periodic, repeatable phenomena (e.g., diurnal cycles) to mark out apparently equal intervals. Without such periodic return, we cannot produce a convenient or standing measure of duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular periodical appearances (sun, moon, seasonal signs) are proper measures of time
rubrics_metrics.description: The diurnal and annual revolutions of the sun (and other regular, universally observable periodical appearances) are the most proper measures of time for mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that any constant, regular, universally observable periodic phenomenon would serve equally well (e.g., plant blooming, bird migrations, ague fits). He notes that blind people can measure years by seasonal signs other than motion, showing motion is not essential to temporal measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: No two parts of duration can be certainly known to be equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Because two distinct portions of succession cannot be directly compared by bringing them together, we cannot demonstrably know that two portions of duration are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even pendulums or planetary motions thought regular cannot be proved to produce exactly equal successive swings or revolutions, since causes and media may vary. All temporal measures rest on seeming or presumed equality judged by memory of trains of ideas plus probable reasons, not infallible demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time is not simply the measure of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is mistaken to define time as the measure of motion; measuring motion requires consideration of space (and bulk) as well as time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke emphasizes that motion only helps measure duration insofar as it produces regular periodical appearances. If motion were irregular or not circular, it would not serve as a measure of time; thus time and motion are distinct concepts and require separate considerations (space and bulk for motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of time (minutes/hours/days/years) are conventions, not necessary parts of duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Units like minutes, hours, days, and years are measures we apply by custom; they are not intrinsically necessary to the notion of duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different cultures might use different temporal units; without regular periodical returns we could not communicate durations, but the particular units are conventional analogues to spatial standards (feet, cubits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal measures can be applied to durations antecedent to their existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once we have an idea of a period (e.g., a year), we can apply that measure in thought to durations before that period or motion existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one can say Abraham was born in a certain Julian year even though the sun’s revolutions did not literally mark that earlier duration. Similarly, we can apply a yard or mile to imagined spatial extents beyond actual bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: The idea of eternity derives from the same origin as time
rubrics_metrics.description: Having formed ideas of succession and durations, we can add lengths of duration in thought without bounds to form the idea of eternity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that by repeatedly adding mental measures of duration (e.g., years) we can proceed ad infinitum and thereby conceive of eternity, just as we can conceive very large numbers by successive addition.
